title: The API treats the browser's origin as a presentation detail while the cookie is the whole credential, so any web page can mint tokens and reach the code validator
index_line: T-0074 · CODE_EXEC · wildcard CORS with credentials + SameSite=None refresh cookie → token mint → /validate/code exec · python · corroborated
invariant_violated: The service treated the Origin of a cross-site request as a rendering concern and the session cookie as the only thing worth checking; because the refresh cookie was sent cross-site and the API reflected any origin with credentials, possession of the user's browser became possession of the user's tokens — and those tokens reach an endpoint that executes code by design.

mechanism.does: a victim holding a Langflow session loads an attacker page that issues a cross-origin request to the token-refresh endpoint with credentials
the refresh endpoint accepts the ambient session cookie and issues a fresh access/refresh token pair; it performs no origin or CSRF validation
the refresh cookie is SameSite=None, so the browser attaches it to the attacker's cross-site request — the cookie's own scope policy is the guard that fails
the response is readable cross-origin because Access-Control-Allow-Origin reflects the attacker's origin together with Allow-Credentials: true
the attacker replays the minted bearer token against POST /api/v1/validate/code
the validator exec()s the submitted function definitions — default arguments and decorators evaluate during validation — running attacker code in the server process

source.http.cookie.value: the SameSite=None refresh-token cookie, attached by the victim's browser to the attacker's cross-site request

sink.eval.value: /api/v1/validate/code: the validator exec()s the submitted function definitions, so default arguments and decorators run

guard.none.value: no CSRF token and no Origin allowlist on the refresh endpoint; the CORS policy reflects arbitrary origins with credentials

oracle.channel.value: the fresh token pair lands in a response body made readable by Access-Control-Allow-Origin + Allow-Credentials

preconditions.expr: the service configures permissive CORS with credentials or a SameSite=None session cookie
the API and its refresh endpoint answer over HTTP
the CORS layer reflects an arbitrary Origin while allowing credentials

success: a cross-origin request from a page the tester controls returns a token pair in a body the browser exposes
the minted token is accepted by /api/v1/validate/code and the submitted function's side effect runs
failure_like: Access-Control-Allow-Origin echoes only a fixed allowlist and Allow-Credentials is absent
the refresh endpoint requires a CSRF token or a non-ambient header credential
false_positive: a wildcard ACAO on endpoints that carry no credentials is not this bug — require Allow-Credentials with a reflected origin AND a credential-bearing response
a 200 from /validate/code without executing the tester's side effect is an auth wall, not code execution

hazards: any SPA/API split where the cookie is the credential and CORS is configured for developer convenience
SameSite=None is the tell: it exists so third-party front-ends can call the API, which is exactly the property being abused
the code-execution endpoint does not need to be new — the record is about borrowing the user's ambient authority to reach it
non_transfers: token-in-header designs with no ambient cookie
refresh endpoints that validate Origin against a fixed allowlist or require a CSRF token

evidence.target: Langflow <= 1.6.9 (FastAPI backend), CORS + refresh-cookie chain to /api/v1/validate/code (CVE-2025-34291)

provenance.author: Obsidian Security Research
provenance.corroborates: CVE-2025-34291: Langflow allows cross-origin requests with credentials from any source, the refresh endpoint lacks CSRF defences with a SameSite=None cookie, and the /api/v1/validate/code endpoint executes submitted code by design — the chain yields one-click account takeover and RCE

provenance.author: VulnCheck
provenance.corroborates: CWE-346 origin validation error: allow_origins=* combined with allow_credentials=True and a SameSite=None refresh cookie lets an attacker-controlled origin obtain fresh access/refresh token pairs, which reach the built-in code-execution endpoint
